name: Singapore
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the integrated regulator and central bank, supervising banks through the Banking Act, the Financial Services and Markets Act and its binding Notices, alongside Guidelines that it expects banks to follow. Staff training obligations are concentrated in the AML/CFT Notice 626 (regular training for all employees and officers), the Technology Risk Management Guidelines (annual security awareness), the Individual Accountability and Conduct Guidelines and the Fair Dealing Guidelines. Representatives selling investment products face exam and yearly CPD rules. STRO receives suspicious transaction reports, the PDPC enforces the PDPA, IRAS runs FATCA/CRS and FIDReC resolves retail disputes.

regulators.name: Monetary Authority of Singapore
regulators.role: Central bank and integrated financial regulator; licenses and supervises banks and issues binding Notices and supervisory Guidelines on AML/CFT, conduct, governance and technology risk.

regulators.name: Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office, Singapore Police Force
regulators.role: Singapore's financial intelligence unit; receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and terrorism financing disclosures filed through SONAR.

regulators.name: Personal Data Protection Commission
regulators.role: Administers and enforces the Personal Data Protection Act, including accountability and data breach notification obligations.

regulators.name: Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
regulators.role: Competent authority for FATCA and CRS; receives account reports from Singaporean financial institutions and sets compliance expectations.

regulators.name: Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre
regulators.role: Independent dispute resolution scheme that banks serving retail customers must join; handles complaints the bank has not resolved.

programs.title: Singapore | MAS Notice 626 AML/CFT Awareness
programs.why: MAS Notice 626 is binding on every bank in Singapore and expressly requires regular, appropriate AML/CFT training for all employees and officers, including those abroad. MAS guidance adds that new joiners should be trained soon after hiring, that refreshers should follow, and that records and effectiveness checks should be kept for audit.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Banks must take appropriate steps so that employees and officers, in Singapore or abroad, are regularly and appropriately trained on AML/CFT laws, CDD measures, detecting and reporting suspicious transactions, and current typologies.

references.title: Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

references.title: Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992
references.note: Anyone who, through their work, knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect property is linked to crime must file a suspicious transaction report with STRO; failing to do so can be an offence.

programs.title: Singapore | Countering Terrorism Financing under the TSOFA and Notice 626
programs.why: Notice 626 training covers terrorism financing as well as money laundering, and the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act places a personal duty on everyone in Singapore to disclose terrorist property and related transactions. Staff need to recognise TF indicators and know how to disclose through STRO.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Banks must take appropriate steps so that employees and officers, in Singapore or abroad, are regularly and appropriately trained on AML/CFT laws, CDD measures, detecting and reporting suspicious transactions, and current typologies.

references.title: Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act 2002
references.note: Anyone in Singapore (and Singapore citizens abroad) holding terrorist property or information about related transactions must disclose it to the Police; good-faith disclosure is protected.

references.title: Suspicious Transaction Reporting
references.issuer: Singapore Police Force - Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office
references.note: STRO guidance on who must report, how to file through SONAR and how terrorism financing disclosures can be made by STR.

programs.title: Singapore | Proliferation Financing Risk and UN Sanctions
programs.why: Since the July 2025 amendments, Notice 626 requires banks to bring proliferation financing into their enterprise-wide risk assessment and to consider Singapore's national PF risk assessment. Combined with the MAS sanctions regulations for DPRK and Iran, staff in exposed roles must understand PF red flags, though no separate PF course is prescribed.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: The 30 June 2025 amendment (in force 1 July 2025) adds proliferation financing to institutional risk assessments and points banks to the national ML, TF and PF risk assessments.

references.title: Regulations for Targeted Financial Sanctions
references.note: Country-specific Financial Services and Markets (Sanctions and Freezing of Assets of Persons) Regulations 2023 require immediate freezing, a ban on dealings with designated persons and reporting to MAS; breaches are offences.

references.title: Lists of Designated Individuals and Entities
references.note: MAS page pointing to the UN lists that banks must screen against, including the reinstated UN Iran sanctions list (September 2025).

programs.title: Singapore | Customer Due Diligence under MAS Notice 626
programs.why: Notice 626 sets detailed CDD steps (identifying and verifying customers, beneficial owners and persons acting for them, understanding purpose and nature of the relationship) and its training paragraph expressly lists CDD measures as a required training topic.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks

programs.title: Singapore | Enhanced CDD for Higher-Risk Customers (Notice 626)
programs.why: Notice 626 requires enhanced measures for higher-risk customers and situations, and the 2025 amendments added shell company risk characteristics and enhanced mitigation for certain digital token transfers. Staff who apply these measures must be competent to do so; the general training duty covers them.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Enhanced CDD applies to higher-risk customers, PEPs and higher-risk countries; 2025 changes added higher-risk shell company indicators and digital token transfer safeguards.

references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

programs.title: Singapore | Ongoing Monitoring and COSMIC Information Sharing
programs.why: Banks must keep CDD information current and monitor relationships throughout their life. Prescribed banks on the COSMIC platform must also factor information received from other banks into ongoing monitoring and EDD, so the relevant staff need to understand both duties.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Requires ongoing monitoring of business relations; prescribed banks must take COSMIC information into account in monitoring and enhanced due diligence.

references.title: Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

programs.title: Singapore | Beneficial Ownership Identification (Notice 626)
programs.why: Notice 626 requires banks to identify beneficial owners and take reasonable measures to verify their identities; MAS confirmed in 2025 that this verification duty remains. Staff handling legal persons and arrangements must be able to unwind ownership and control structures.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Identify the natural persons who ultimately own or control a customer and take reasonable measures to verify them.

references.title: Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

programs.title: Singapore | Politically Exposed Persons under Notice 626
programs.why: Notice 626 requires banks to determine whether customers or beneficial owners are PEPs and to apply enhanced measures, including senior management approval and source-of-wealth checks, for higher-risk PEP relationships. Staff must recognise PEPs and their associates.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: PEP determination and enhanced measures, including senior management approval and establishing source of wealth and funds.

programs.title: Singapore | MAS Targeted Financial Sanctions Compliance
programs.why: MAS gives effect to UN Security Council targeted financial sanctions through regulations under the Financial Services and Markets Act. Banks must freeze assets immediately, refuse dealings with designated persons and report to MAS, with criminal penalties for breaches, so staff must understand screening and escalation.

programs.title: Singapore | Asset Freezing under the FSM Sanctions Regulations
programs.why: When a person is designated, banks must freeze funds without delay and notify MAS. This needs operations and compliance staff who know the freezing, reporting and licensing steps under the country-specific regulations and the TSOFA.

programs.why: Singapore implements UNSC sanctions regimes (including DPRK, Iran, Libya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Yemen and DR Congo) through MAS regulations. The UN Iran list was reinstated in September 2025, so screening staff must keep track of list changes.

programs.title: Singapore | Suspicious Transaction Reporting to STRO
programs.why: Section 45 of the CDSA makes failure to report suspicion an offence for anyone in employment, and Notice 626 requires STR policies plus training on detecting and reporting suspicious transactions. Since August 2024 reports must be filed through SONAR.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Training must cover how to detect and report suspicious transactions.

references.title: Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992
references.note: Anyone who, through their work, knows or has reasonable grounds to suspect property is linked to crime must file a suspicious transaction report with STRO; failing to do so can be an offence.

references.note: Section 45 disclosures must be filed electronically through STRO's SONAR system, with an email fallback when SONAR is down.

references.title: Suspicious Transaction Reporting
references.issuer: Singapore Police Force - Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office
references.note: STRO guidance on who must report, how to file through SONAR and how terrorism financing disclosures can be made by STR.

programs.title: Singapore | Transaction Monitoring and Alert Handling
programs.why: Notice 626 requires banks to monitor transactions for unusual or suspicious activity and to investigate and document alerts. Analysts need the skills to assess alerts and decide on escalation; no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Ongoing monitoring of transactions, with unusual or suspicious activity examined and documented.

references.title: Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

programs.title: Singapore | Correspondent Banking under Notice 626
audience: Correspondent banking and FI relationship teams
programs.why: Notice 626 sets specific measures for cross-border correspondent relationships and bars relationships with shell banks or poorly supervised respondents. Staff who onboard and review respondent banks must apply these measures.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Assessment of respondent banks' AML/CFT controls and supervision, senior approval, and a ban on shell bank relationships.

programs.title: Singapore | AML/CFT/PF Risk-Based Approach and Risk Assessment
programs.why: Banks must identify, assess and mitigate their ML/TF risks, and since July 2025 PF risks, taking account of Singapore's national risk assessments. Those who design and run the risk assessment need to understand the methodology and inputs.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Enterprise-wide risk assessment covering customers, countries, products, services, transactions and delivery channels, now including PF and national risk assessments.

programs.title: Singapore | AML Record Keeping under Notice 626
programs.why: Notice 626 requires CDD and transaction records to be kept so they can reconstruct transactions and be produced promptly to authorities. Operations and compliance staff need to know what to keep and for how long.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Sets record retention and retrieval requirements for CDD data and transactions.

programs.title: Singapore | AML/CFT for Frontline and Branch Staff
programs.why: The Notice 626 training duty extends to all employees, and MAS guidance asks banks to pitch content to each job's responsibilities. Frontline staff therefore need practical training on CDD at onboarding, red flags and internal escalation.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Banks must take appropriate steps so that employees and officers, in Singapore or abroad, are regularly and appropriately trained on AML/CFT laws, CDD measures, detecting and reporting suspicious transactions, and current typologies.

references.title: Guidelines to MAS Notice 626 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
references.note: Explains MAS expectations behind the Notice, including tailoring training scope and frequency to the bank's risks and each role, training new joiners promptly, refresher cycles and keeping training records.

programs.title: Singapore | AML/CFT Oversight for Board and Senior Management
programs.why: Notice 626 training covers officers as well as employees, and senior management must approve the bank's AML/CFT policies, risk assessment and higher-risk relationships. Under MAS accountability expectations, senior leaders must understand the bank's financial crime exposure.

references.title: MAS Notice 626 Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism - Banks
references.note: Applies to officers as well as employees.

references.title: Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct

programs.title: Singapore | Anti-Bribery under the Prevention of Corruption Act
programs.why: The Prevention of Corruption Act criminalises private-sector bribery and reaches Singapore citizens abroad, and corruption proceeds are predicate offences under the CDSA. No statutory training duty was verified, but awareness is standard good practice for banks.

references.title: Prevention of Corruption Act 1960
references.note: Criminalises giving and receiving bribes in the public and private sectors, with extraterritorial reach for Singapore citizens; it does not itself prescribe staff training.

programs.title: Singapore | Fraud Reporting and Scam Prevention (Notice 641 and SRF)
audience: Customer service and contact centre staff
programs.why: Banks must report material fraud and suspicious activities to MAS under Notice 641 and, under the Shared Responsibility Framework, run real-time fraud surveillance and meet anti-phishing duties or bear customers' losses. Staff must be competent to detect, handle and report fraud; no specific course is prescribed.

references.title: MAS Notice 641 Reporting of Suspicious Activities and Incidents of Fraud
references.note: Banks must report to MAS suspicious activities and fraud incidents material to their safety, soundness or reputation within five working days of discovery, separately from STRs to STRO.

references.title: Guidelines on Shared Responsibility Framework
references.issuer: Monetary Authority of Singapore and Infocomm Media Development Authority
references.note: Sets anti-phishing duties for banks and telcos, including real-time fraud surveillance, with the bank first in line to bear losses if it breaches its duties.

programs.title: Singapore | Corporate Governance under the MAS CG Guidelines
programs.why: The MAS Corporate Governance Guidelines set expectations for board composition, committees, risk oversight and disclosure for locally incorporated banks. Directors and governance staff need to understand them; training is addressed separately for directors.

references.title: Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Designated Financial Holding Companies, Banks, Direct Insurers, Reinsurers and Captive Insurers which are incorporated in Singapore
references.note: Expects induction and suitable training for new directors (especially those without prior financial institution board experience), ongoing development for all directors, and disclosure of these arrangements.

programs.title: Singapore | Director Induction and Continuing Development
programs.why: MAS expects banks to provide induction and suitable training for new directors, particularly those without prior financial institution board experience, and ongoing development for all directors, and to disclose these arrangements. MAS leaves the content to each bank.

references.title: Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Designated Financial Holding Companies, Banks, Direct Insurers, Reinsurers and Captive Insurers which are incorporated in Singapore
references.note: Expects induction and suitable training for new directors (especially those without prior financial institution board experience), ongoing development for all directors, and disclosure of these arrangements.

programs.title: Singapore | Senior Manager Accountability (IAC Guidelines)
programs.why: The IAC Guidelines expect clearly identified senior managers who are fit and proper, with defined responsibilities and accountability for staff conduct. Senior managers must understand their personal accountability; no separate course is prescribed for them.

references.title: Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct
references.note: Five outcomes covering senior manager identification, fitness and accountability, governance structure, material risk personnel and the conduct framework for all staff.

programs.title: Singapore | Code of Conduct and Conduct Framework (IAC Outcome 5)
programs.why: Under Outcome 5 of the IAC Guidelines, the board and senior management must have a framework that sets conduct standards for all employees and communicates them through a code of conduct, onboarding and regular training, with lessons from misconduct shared.

references.title: Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct
references.note: Conduct standards for all staff must be set and communicated, including through onboarding and regular training.

references.title: FAQs on Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct
references.note: MAS expects conduct expectations to be communicated at hiring, during onboarding and through regular training, and cites training completion rates as a board-level indicator.

programs.title: Singapore | Material Risk Personnel Training (IAC Outcome 4)
programs.why: Outcome 4 of the IAC Guidelines expects banks to give material risk personnel regular training on the competencies their roles need, the risks of their activities and expected standards of conduct, alongside risk-aligned incentives.

references.title: Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct
references.note: Material risk personnel should receive regular training on role competencies, risk implications and proper conduct.

references.title: FAQs on Guidelines on Individual Accountability and Conduct
references.note: MAS expects conduct expectations to be communicated at hiring, during onboarding and through regular training, and cites training completion rates as a board-level indicator.

programs.title: Singapore | MAS Fair Dealing Outcomes
programs.why: The revised Fair Dealing Guidelines (May 2024) hold the board and senior management accountable for delivering fair dealing outcomes, including training staff and representatives on regulatory requirements, products and fair dealing so customers are treated fairly.

references.title: Guidelines on Fair Dealing - Board and Senior Management Responsibilities for Delivering Fair Dealing Outcomes to Customers [FSG-G04]
references.note: Board and senior management must embed fair dealing outcomes, including ongoing training of staff and representatives and training on products before they are sold.

references.title: Thematic review of Financial Institutions' recruitment and onboarding training of representatives
references.note: MAS findings and good practices on onboarding training and supervision of new representatives before they advise customers independently.

programs.title: Singapore | Complaint Handling under the Fair Dealing Guidelines
programs.why: One of the fair dealing outcomes is that customers' complaints are handled independently, effectively and promptly. Staff who receive and resolve complaints must be competent in the bank's process and in referral to FIDReC.

references.title: Guidelines on Fair Dealing - Board and Senior Management Responsibilities for Delivering Fair Dealing Outcomes to Customers [FSG-G04]
references.note: Includes the outcome that complaints are handled in an independent, effective and prompt manner.

programs.title: Singapore | FIDReC Dispute Resolution
programs.why: Banks serving retail customers must belong to FIDReC under the Financial Services and Markets (Dispute Resolution Schemes) Regulations 2023. Customers may escalate unresolved complaints there after the bank's final reply, so complaint staff must know the process and timelines.

references.title: Consultation on Expanding FIDReC Membership to Payment Service Providers
references.note: Confirms the FIDReC dispute resolution scheme framework under the Financial Services and Markets (Dispute Resolution Schemes) Regulations 2023, which banks serving retail customers must join; proposes extending it to payment firms.

programs.title: Singapore | Mis-selling Prevention and Representative Onboarding
programs.why: MAS expects representatives not to advise customers independently until supervisors are satisfied they are competent, and its 2025 thematic review set out good practice for recruitment and onboarding training. These expectations target mis-selling risk.

references.title: Thematic review of Financial Institutions' recruitment and onboarding training of representatives
references.note: MAS findings and good practices on onboarding training and supervision of new representatives before they advise customers independently.

references.title: Guidelines on Fair Dealing - Board and Senior Management Responsibilities for Delivering Fair Dealing Outcomes to Customers [FSG-G04]
references.note: Representatives should be trained on products before marketing them and supervised until competent.

programs.title: Singapore | Banking Secrecy and Customer Confidentiality
programs.why: Section 47 of the Banking Act restricts disclosure of customer information by banks and their officers to the cases set out in the Third Schedule, and even confirming that someone is a customer can be a breach. Every officer handling customer data must understand these limits.

references.title: Banking Act 1970
references.note: Banking secrecy: banks and their officers may disclose customer information only as the Act and its Third Schedule allow.

references.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
references.note: General personal data protection duties that apply alongside banking secrecy.

programs.title: Singapore | Representative Competency and CPD (FAA-N26)
programs.why: Banks are exempt financial advisers, and their appointed representatives must pass the required examinations and complete yearly continuing professional development, including ethics and rules content, under Notice FAA-N26. The bank must track and record compliance.

references.title: Notice FAA-N26 Competency Requirements for Representatives of Financial Advisers
references.note: Representatives of licensed and exempt financial advisers (including banks) must meet examination requirements and complete yearly continuing professional development, including ethics and rules content; the principal must keep records.

references.title: Guidelines on Fair Dealing - Board and Senior Management Responsibilities for Delivering Fair Dealing Outcomes to Customers [FSG-G04]
references.note: Expects structured, continuing training of representatives on products and suitability.

programs.title: Singapore | Information Security Awareness (MAS TRM Guidelines)
programs.why: The MAS TRM Guidelines expressly expect an annual IT security awareness training programme for all staff, contractors and service providers with access to the bank's information assets, and training for the board. MAS supervises banks against these Guidelines.

references.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines
references.note: Section 3.6 expects a comprehensive IT security awareness programme, run at least annually for staff, contractors and service providers with access to information assets, covering the threat landscape, policies and personal responsibilities; the board should also be trained.

programs.title: Singapore | Cyber Security Awareness (MAS TRM Guidelines)
programs.why: The same TRM training programme must cover the current cyber threat landscape and its implications, so all staff understand their role in defending against attacks. MAS allows content and frequency above the annual minimum to be tailored to different audiences.

references.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines
references.note: Section 3.6 expects a comprehensive IT security awareness programme, run at least annually for staff, contractors and service providers with access to information assets, covering the threat landscape, policies and personal responsibilities; the board should also be trained.

references.title: Notice FSM-N06 Cyber Hygiene
references.note: Mandatory baseline cyber controls: securing administrative accounts, security patching, baseline security standards, network perimeter defence, anti-malware and multi-factor authentication.

programs.title: Singapore | Technology and Cyber Risk Management (FSM-N05, FSM-N06)
programs.why: Notices FSM-N05 and FSM-N06 set legally binding technology resilience and cyber hygiene controls, and the TRM Guidelines describe the governance framework expected around them. IT and risk staff must be competent to operate these controls.

references.title: Notice FSM-N05 Technology Risk Management
references.note: Requires high availability and recoverability of critical systems (recovery within four hours), MAS notification of relevant IT incidents within one hour of discovery and a root-cause report within 14 days.

references.title: Notice FSM-N06 Cyber Hygiene
references.note: Mandatory baseline cyber controls: securing administrative accounts, security patching, baseline security standards, network perimeter defence, anti-malware and multi-factor authentication.

references.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines
references.note: Framework guidance on technology risk governance, IT and cyber risk management, read together with the FSM-N05 and FSM-N06 Notices.

programs.title: Singapore | PDPA Data Protection Obligations
programs.why: Section 12 of the PDPA requires organisations to develop data protection policies and to communicate them to staff; the PDPC has treated staff training as a necessary means of doing so and has penalised organisations that failed to. Banks must also appoint a data protection officer.

references.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
references.note: Organisations must communicate their data protection policies and practices to staff; PDPC decisions treat training as the usual way to do this.

references.title: Data Protection Obligations under the PDPA
references.note: PDPC overview of the accountability obligation, including appointing a data protection officer and putting policies and practices in place.

programs.title: Singapore | Phishing and Scam Awareness (Shared Responsibility Framework)
programs.why: Under the Shared Responsibility Framework, banks carry losses from phishing scams if they breach their duties, and the TRM awareness programme must cover the cyber threat landscape. Staff need to recognise social engineering against both the bank and its customers.

references.title: Guidelines on Shared Responsibility Framework
references.issuer: Monetary Authority of Singapore and Infocomm Media Development Authority
references.note: Sets anti-phishing duties for banks and telcos, including real-time fraud surveillance, with the bank first in line to bear losses if it breaches its duties.

references.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines
references.note: Awareness training must reflect the current cyber threat landscape.

programs.title: Singapore | IT Incident Notification to MAS (FSM-N05)
programs.why: FSM-N05 requires banks to notify MAS of relevant IT incidents within one hour of discovery and to submit a root-cause and impact report within 14 days. Incident responders must know the thresholds and the escalation path.

references.title: Notice FSM-N05 Technology Risk Management
references.note: Requires high availability and recoverability of critical systems (recovery within four hours), MAS notification of relevant IT incidents within one hour of discovery and a root-cause report within 14 days.

programs.title: Singapore | PDPA Data Breach Notification
programs.why: The PDPA requires organisations to assess suspected breaches promptly and, once a breach is notifiable, to notify the PDPC within three calendar days and affected individuals as soon as practicable. Response teams must know the assessment criteria and timelines.

references.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
references.note: Data breach notification obligation.

references.title: Guide on Managing and Notifying Data Breaches under the PDPA
references.note: Once a breach is assessed as notifiable, the PDPC must be told within three calendar days and affected individuals as soon as practicable; post-breach steps include staff training.

programs.title: Singapore | Operational Resilience of Critical Business Services
programs.why: MAS expects banks to identify critical business services, set service recovery time objectives and test them, while FSM-N05 caps recovery of critical systems at four hours. Owners of critical services must understand these targets.

references.title: Guidelines on Business Continuity Management
references.note: Critical business services need defined recovery objectives, dependency mapping, regular testing and audit at least every three years.

references.title: Notice FSM-N05 Technology Risk Management
references.note: Requires high availability and recoverability of critical systems (recovery within four hours), MAS notification of relevant IT incidents within one hour of discovery and a root-cause report within 14 days.

programs.title: Singapore | ICT Risk Management under the TRM Guidelines
programs.why: The TRM Guidelines and FSM-N05 require board-approved technology risk governance and controls over IT systems, and MAS consulted in 2026 on extending the Notice to more areas such as IT asset inventories. Technology staff must stay competent as these rules change.

references.title: Technology Risk Management Guidelines
references.note: Board and senior management oversight of technology risk, with IT risk management controls across the system life cycle.

references.title: Notice FSM-N05 Technology Risk Management
references.note: Requires high availability and recoverability of critical systems (recovery within four hours), MAS notification of relevant IT incidents within one hour of discovery and a root-cause report within 14 days.

programs.title: Singapore | Outsourcing Risk Management (MAS Notice 658)
programs.why: Notice 658, in force since 11 December 2024, and the Guidelines on Outsourcing (Banks) set binding requirements for due diligence, contracts, oversight and exit of outsourced services. Staff who manage service providers must be competent in them; no separate training is prescribed.

references.title: MAS Notice 658 Management of Outsourced Relevant Services for Banks
references.note: Binding requirements for managing the risks of outsourced relevant services, to be read with the Guidelines on Outsourcing (Banks).

references.title: Banking Act 1970
references.note: Banking secrecy: banks and their officers may disclose customer information only as the Act and its Third Schedule allow.

programs.title: Singapore | Business Continuity Management (MAS BCM Guidelines)
programs.why: The 2022 BCM Guidelines expect a training programme, reviewed annually, so that staff with business continuity roles understand their responsibilities, alongside regular testing of plans against severe but plausible scenarios.

references.title: Guidelines on Business Continuity Management
references.note: Expects a BCM training programme for staff with BCM roles, reviewed annually, plus testing and periodic audit.

programs.title: Singapore | FATCA Compliance under the Singapore-US IGA
programs.why: Under the Singapore-US Model 1 IGA, Reporting Singaporean Financial Institutions must register, perform due diligence and report US accounts to IRAS by 31 May each year. IRAS expects internal controls to support this, which requires competent staff.

programs.title: Singapore | Common Reporting Standard (CRS) Compliance
programs.why: The CRS Regulations require Reporting SGFIs to register, perform due diligence on all financial accounts and report to IRAS. IRAS expects proportionate internal controls, independent review and five-year record retention, so staff must be competent in self-certification and reporting.

references.title: Getting It Right - CRS Compliance
references.note: IRAS expects proportionate entity, process and reporting-level controls against 23 hallmarks, independent periodic review and five-year retention of CRS records.

notes: MAS Notice 626 was reissued under the Financial Services and Markets Act on 28 March 2024 (effective 1 April 2024) and amended on 30 June 2025 (effective 1 July 2025) to add proliferation financing risk assessment, use of national risk assessments, higher-risk shell company indicators and digital token transfer safeguards.
COSMIC, the MAS bank-to-bank information sharing platform, now applies to prescribed banks, which must factor shared information into monitoring and enhanced due diligence.
From 1 August 2024, suspicious transaction reports under section 45 of the CDSA must be filed electronically through STRO's SONAR system.

Technology Risk Management Notice 644 and Cyber Hygiene Notice 655 were cancelled from 10 May 2024 and replaced by Notices FSM-N05 and FSM-N06; MAS consulted in 2026 on further amendments to the technology risk notices.
Notice 658 and the Guidelines on Outsourcing (Banks) took effect on 11 December 2024, replacing the earlier outsourcing guidelines for banks.
The Shared Responsibility Framework for phishing scams took effect on 16 December 2024, including a real-time fraud surveillance duty for banks.
MAS revised the Fair Dealing Guidelines in May 2024 and published a thematic review on representatives' recruitment and onboarding training in December 2025.
The UN Iran sanctions list was reinstated on 27 September 2025; banks must reflect this in sanctions screening under the MAS regulations.
MAS consulted in 2026 on extending FIDReC membership to payment service providers and on amendments to the bank corporate governance regulations; neither was confirmed in force at review.
IRAS requires FATCA XML submissions to follow schema version 2.0.1 from 1 January 2027, and has flagged CRS XML schema changes for later reporting years.
